extracted.intended_audience: students and writers of fiction; readers interested in novel craft and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on creating and evaluating characters and narrative method in novels, especially the flat vs round distinction and choice of point of view. Emphasises how characters must adapt to plot, moral, atmosphere and how the novelist controls reader acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-as-centre (character-driven novel)
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel in which 'a character is everything and is given freest play' — the character may dominate the book and plot be perfunctory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Moll Flanders — 'Nothing matters but the heroine — she stands in an open space like a tree.' When a character is central the author may permit plot to be slight; evaluate whether the central character sustains interest and coherence without an elaborate plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character reality (novelist's knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: A character in a book is real when the novelist knows everything about it: 'He may not choose to tell us all he knows…but he will give us the feeling that though the character has not been explained, it is explicable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: the reader should get the feeling of underlying, coherent knowledge even when details are withheld. The novelist should convey that characters are 'explicable' — otherwise they feel artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency with the novel's laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel is a work of art with its own laws; characters are real when they live 'in accordance with such laws.' Characters need not match daily life exactly, only be convincing within the book's internal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not penalize departures from daily-life probability if they serve the novel's internal aesthetic. Use the 'aesthetic reply' when judging realism: focus on convincingness given the novel's own laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization (fit characters to other novel aspects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must adapt to other requirements of fiction (plot, moral, fellow characters, atmosphere); they will have to 'fit in' with these elements and may be constrained by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether characters operate believably within the novel's plot, moral stance and group of characters. Example contrast: Jane Austen's interdependent characters vs Defoe's isolated heroine (Moll).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat character definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters (humours/types/caricatures) are constructed around a single idea or quality and 'can be expressed in one sentence' (e.g. 'I never will desert Mr. Micawber').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize flat characters by their single-phrase summability and lack of private complexities. They are useful as readily recognized, durable elements and for comic effect; but as serious/tragic long-term figures they risk boredom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round character definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters are complex, capable of development and surprise; 'the test of a round character is whether it is capable of surprising in a convincing way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge roundness by convincing unpredictability and depth. If a character never surprises, it is flat; if it surprises but doesn't convince, it's a failed attempt at roundness. Examples: principal characters in War and Peace, Dostoevsky characters, Becky Sharp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are easily recognized on re-entry, never need reintroduction, are easily remembered, and provide a 'comforting' permanence for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use flat characters when you need clarity, economy, recurring comic/attributive effect or memorable types (examples: many Dickens and Wells characters). They are 'little luminous disks' that help the reader immediately grasp function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantages / misuses of flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat rendering can falsify life by selecting a few facets and discarding the rest, and a serious/tragic flat character is apt to bore; in biography the 'novelist's touch' that flattens is particularly reprehensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing complex human beings to single-sentence formulas when the work needs psychological/verisimilar depth. Critics (e.g., Norman Douglas) argue this 'falsifies life' — beware when realism is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of flat and round for balance
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex novel often requires both flat and round characters; their collisions and interactions 'parallel life' more accurately than only one kind would.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a novel's cast by whether the mixture of types and complexities harmonizes — e.g., Dickens/Wells use flat types energized by authorial force, while Austen uses smaller but highly organized characters that function together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of plausibility by integration (interdependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters that are tightly woven into a social fabric (e.g., Jane Austen's Miss Bates tied to Highbury) are more plausible as a whole; isolated characters (e.g., Moll) can be transplanted without breaking the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether removing or relocating a character would collapse plausibility; highly interdependent characters should evidence internal ties (family, setting, recurring relationships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial control vs character autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are creations inside a creation and may 'run away' or 'get out of hand'; if given too much freedom they can 'kick the book to pieces', while too much control can cause them to 'die' or the work to decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For production: balance freedom and control—allow characters believable agency but keep them aligned enough with the novel's scheme to preserve coherence. For evaluation: note signs of characters undermining or being stifled by the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view selection as a central device
rubrics_metrics.description: The point of view (relation of narrator to story) is a fundamental device: the novelist may describe from outside (impartial/partial onlooker), assume omniscience, place himself in the position of a character (limited/first-person), or adopt intermediate attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a POV that supports desired knowledge of characters and persuasive effect. Evaluate whether the chosen POV 'bounces the reader into accepting what he says' — narrative authority and method must convince the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative authority / 'bouncing' the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's power to 'bounce the reader into accepting what he says' (i.e., to make the reader accept the invented world and character truths) is central to method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the strength of the narrative voice and technique in eliciting reader belief. Examples: Dickens' omniscience in Bleak House and Wells' energetic handling that makes flat figures seem alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictional knowledge compensates for life's dimness
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction can give perfect knowledge of people that life cannot; 'in the novel we can know people perfectly' and fiction 'goes beyond the evidence', offering a form of truth different from history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging realism, consider whether the novel's deeper 'compensation' for life's incompleteness is successful: does the author plausibly supply the 'something beyond the evidence'?
